conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim is supported, citing strong evidence from the MAP.3 randomized controlled trial showing a significant reduction in invasive breast cancer incidence, as well as endorsement in professional guidance from ASCO.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported, not false. The strongest evidence is the MAP.3 randomized, placebo-controlled trial in postmenopausal women at moderately/increased breast-cancer risk. Its primary publication concluded that exemestane **significantly reduced invasive breast cancers** during a median three-year follow-up. Reported trial summaries describe a roughly **65% relative reduction** in invasive breast cancer at 35 months in 4,560 participants.

This is evidence of reduced **incidence** (new diagnosed cancers), which is exactly the claim—not proof that exemestane reduces breast-cancer mortality or all-cause mortality. The relatively short follow-up also limits certainty about the durability of benefit after stopping treatment and long-term harms.

The finding has been incorporated into professional guidance: ASCO’s update identifies exemestane 25 mg daily for five years as one of the endocrine options shown in large randomized trials to reduce breast-cancer incidence in postmenopausal women at increased risk. The balance is individualized: exemestane lowers estrogen and can harm bone; a MAP.3 bone substudy found worsened age-related bone loss despite calcium and vitamin D.

Lack of an FDA prevention indication would concern regulatory status, not whether the trial demonstrated an incidence reduction.
